questions.question: A four-shard service receives 120,000 writes per second. One shard receives 48% of them. How many writes per second reach that shard?
questions.explanation: Multiply total demand by the hot shard's share: 120,000 x 0.48 = 57,600 writes per second. Fleet average utilization would hide this concentrated pressure.

questions.question: Which invariant matters most while a logical shard moves from one physical owner to another?
options: Every shard must contain the same number of rows
One authoritative owner is named for each routing epoch and acknowledged writes remain reachable
All queries must fan out during migration
The target must accept writes as soon as copying begins
questions.explanation: Versioned single ownership prevents split-brain writes, while the migration protocol must preserve every acknowledged change across copy and cutover.

questions.question: Why can hashing by order_id be a poor shard key for a tenant dashboard even when writes are evenly distributed?
options: Hashing makes order IDs mutable
All orders are sent to the newest time range
One tenant's orders can span every shard, forcing fanout and result merging
A hash key always requires two-phase commit
questions.explanation: Hashing order IDs balances point writes, but it removes tenant locality. A tenant-scoped query may need to contact and merge results from all owners.

questions.question: What is the safest sequence for an online shard migration?
options: Cut over routing, then copy whatever rows are missing
Copy a snapshot, replay ordered changes, verify, fence the old owner, then advance the ownership epoch
Enable writes on both owners indefinitely and compare them later
Delete the source before checking the target
questions.explanation: Snapshot plus ordered catch-up closes the write gap. Verification establishes readiness, and fencing before the atomic epoch change prevents two active writers.

questions.question: The source shard fails halfway through a copy, and the target has not passed verification. What should the operator do?
options: Promote the target because some data is better than none
Hash the target rows again
Recover the source owner or its replica and resume from the durable checkpoint
Send every request to all shards
questions.explanation: An incomplete target is not an authoritative owner. Keep the existing epoch, recover the source path, and resume the idempotent migration from known progress.

questions.question: After cutover to epoch 42, a stale router sends a write to the old source with epoch 41. Which behavior best prevents split brain?
options: The source accepts the write and copies it later
The source rejects the stale epoch or returns a moved response so the router refreshes
The router generates a new request ID on every retry
The directory lowers its epoch to match the router
questions.explanation: Fencing makes stale ownership detectable. The old source must not accept new authoritative writes; the router refreshes and safely retries with the same operation identity.
